pages.title: What the | door keeps
pages.label: Writing
pages.subtitle: Writing from Beirut and elsewhere, collected as it was finished. Read in order or begin anywhere.

blocks.title: Wall, late light
blocks.alt: Thorn-branch shadows on a sunlit plaster wall

blocks.text:
The door remembers
the shape of every leaving:
a hand, a weight, the small
hesitation before the latch.

It keeps no names.
It keeps the draught
that followed you out,
and the light that did not.

My grandmother kept salt in a blue tin
and said the sea was only
a long way of being patient.

I carried the tin through three cities.
It never emptied.
Each time I opened it
the room smelled of that distance,
and I forgave something.

pages.title: A guest in my own language
pages.label: Essay

blocks.text: I learned to pray in one language and to apologise in another. For years I thought this was a problem to be solved, as if a person were a house with two front doors and a duty to keep one of them locked.
blocks.note: Written after a reading in Lisbon, March 2025.

blocks.title: Under the leaves
blocks.alt: A man standing beneath a dense green tree, only his legs visible

blocks.text: What I understand now is that each language keeps a different part of me. Arabic holds the kitchen, the stairwell, the voices that called up to a balcony. English holds the desk. When I write in one and think in the other, something is lost, and something is also kept that would not have survived the trip any other way.
A translator once told me the work is not carrying a sentence across a river. It is building a second house with the same light in it. I have been building for a long time. Some rooms are finished.

blocks.title: Through the gate
blocks.alt: A white cat seen through iron bars in a stone courtyard

blocks.text: It is the same window every morning and never the same. Today the neighbour's washing, a bar of sun on the sill, a dog deciding.
I keep thinking the view is the thing that stays. It is only the frame that stays.

blocks.title: The road in
blocks.alt: A road curving through pine hills under a pale sky

blocks.text:
Before the street begins
the street is a held breath.
A bin lid. A scooter, far.

I stand at the kettle
listening to the city
make up its mind
to be a city again.

No one is watching.
This is the best of it:
the whole day
still unspoken.
Two shirts, a blue tin, a charger for a phone I no longer own. A map of a city I left. A letter I have not decided to read.
The weight is not in the objects.
Noor Rahal writes poems and short prose in English and Arabic. She lives between cities and keeps a notebook in each.
A first collection, The Salt Tin, is in preparation.
